h: Vanbrugh's bridge, a victory column and Churchill's resting place
p: The palace was designed by Sir John Vanbrugh, with help from Nicholas Hawksmoor, and it's the only non-royal, non-episcopal country house in England to hold the title of palace. Out in the park, Vanbrugh's Grand Bridge spans the lake and makes for a wonderful photo, especially with the palace rising behind it. Later, in the 1760s, Capability Brown reshaped the landscape, creating the lake and rolling parkland that so many visitors love today.

On a hill in the park, the Column of Victory rises high, topped by a statue of the 1st Duke of Marlborough. Closer to the palace, the formal Water Terraces with their fountains and the Italian Garden show a different, more ordered style, and the Secret Garden is a quieter, winding spot for a peaceful stroll.

Families often head to the Pleasure Gardens, where the Marlborough Maze is one of the biggest draws, along with a butterfly house and play areas. A little train runs between the palace and the Pleasure Gardens, which is a lifesaver for little legs. Allow most of the day if you want to see the palace, the gardens and a stretch of the park.

Sir Winston Churchill was born at Blenheim in 1874, and he's buried just a short drive away in the churchyard of St Martin's at Bladon, alongside members of his family. Many visitors pay their respects there after a visit. Back in Woodstock, the Oxfordshire Museum is a small but charming place to learn about the area, and the town's tearooms and pubs are perfect for a well-earned rest.
